newsitem.title: NEPAL: Bodies of 11 Nepal air crash victims flown home.
newsitem.headline: Bodies of 11 Nepal air crash victims flown home.

text.p: The bodies of 11 Nepali victims of the world's worst mid-air collision were flown into Nepal's capital Kathmandu on Saturday, to be received by relatives.
Airport officials said wooden coffins containing 11 bodies were flown into the Himalayan kingdom by an Indian Airlines flight from New Delhi.

Nepal said there were 53 Nepalis among the 349 people killed when a Saudi Arabian Airlines jumbo jet collided with a Kazakh Ilyushin Il-76 cargo freighter near the Indian capital, New Delhi, on Tuesday.
"We have nothing left for the family, not even for the funeral," said a grieving Ganga Bahadur Thapa, as he stood beside the coffin of his brother Ana Bahadur Thapa.
Relatives who accompanied the bodies home from India told Reuters that 24 Nepali victims had been identified so far.

Many Nepali workers travel to Saudi Arabia and other Gulf countries in search of employment as manual labourers, plumbers and drivers. Gyaneswar Poudel, one of the bereaved relatives, said more coffins were expected to arrive later on Saturday.
Buddhi Maya Thapa, 37, said she had been unable to identify her husband, Yam Bahadur Thapa, from among the scores of corpses lying in New Delhi's hospitals.
"I could not see his body," she said.

Buddhi Maya said her husband had sold a small piece of land in Nepal's central Nawalparasi district to raise 45,000 rupees ($792) to pay a Nepali recruitment firm which had promised him a job as a vehicle driver in Saudi Arabia.
Buddhi Maya choked as tears streamed down her face and she recalled her husband's last words to her. "I will come after two years," she said he told her. "Take care of the children."
She has four children, three of them girls, and the youngest is just five years old.

Nepali officials estimated that there were about 8,500 Nepalis working in Saudi Arabia, but analysts said the number could be twice as high because many people went there without informing the government.

Nepal is one of the world's 10 poorest countries and remittances from workers abroad are a major source of foreign exchange earnings in a country that receives 60 percent of its development budget in foreign aid.
